newsitem.title: USA: Defense secretary nominee Cohen is poet, novelist.
newsitem.headline: Defense secretary nominee Cohen is poet, novelist.

text.p: Sen. William Cohen, President Bill Clinton's nominee to be defence secretary and the first Republican in Democrat Clinton's Cabinet, is a 24-year veteran of Congress as well as a published poet and spy novelist.
Cohen, 56, is retiring as a U.S. senator from Maine after a career spent largely on defence and intelligence issues -- and on scandals.

Considered a moderate in a Republican party increasingly dominated by conservatives, Cohen said at a White House ceremony at which he was nominated: "I must say that my entire congressional career has been devoted to pursuing a national security policy that is without partisanship."

Cohen was vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee from 1987 to 1991 and of the joint congressional committee that investigated the Iran-Contra affair involving President Ronald Reagan's administration in the late 1980s.

He first came to national attention in 1974 when, as a young congressmen, he served on the House of Representatives Judiciary Committee that approved three articles of impeachment against President Richard Nixon in the Watergate scandal. That action set the stage for Nixon's resignation days later.
Along the way Cohen has published two books of poetry, three non-fiction books and three spy or mystery novels.
He is known for delivering thoughtful arguments in Senate debates, sometimes with poetic allusions.

When the Senate narrowly voted to send U.S. troops into the 1991 Gulf War, for example, Cohen argued that avoiding war with Iraqi President Saddam Hussein then would only risk worse and wider war in the future.
"It would only reserve conflict for our sons and daughters in the future, conflict that would reach well beyond the spinning wheel of the Middle East," he said.
Clinton, announcing Cohen's nomination, said the senator was known for his "discipline, intellect, creative independence and deeply held principles."
He noted that Cohen had helped draft the first Strategic Arms Limitation Treaty in the early 1980s, which called for a cut in U.S.-Soviet warheads to 6,000 on each side.
But despite his long years of legislating defence, intelligence and foreign affairs policy, he has no experience conducting policy or running a federal agency.
After graduation from Boston University Law School in 1965, Cohen was a lawyer, city councilman and then mayor in Bangor, Maine, until his election to the House in 1972.

He gained a career-long reputation for independence two years later when he voted for fellow-Republican Nixon's impeachment at the televised hearings that moved the national drama of the Watergate scandal toward its climax.

Cohen was elected to the Senate in 1978 and showed his independence again as co-chairman of the Senate-House investigation of the Iran-Contra affair. It found that profits from secret arms sales to Iran had been illegally diverted to U.S.-backed Nicaraguan rebels, and concluded that Reagan was lax in overseeing his White House national security team even if he did not authorise the funds diversion.
In an effort to prevent a repetition of such abuses, Cohen proposed that presidents be required to report clandestine operations to Congress within 48 hours.
The Senate approved the 48-hour requirement in 1988 but the House did not and Congress later agreed only to require reports on covert operations in a timely fashion.

On defence, Cohen was a leading opponent of Defence Department plans for large numbers of B-2 stealth bombers, arguing they were too costly and unneeded because cheaper weapons such as cruise missiles could be used instead.
Congress decided in 1993 to buy no more than 20 of the radar-evading bombers although proponents still hope to win at least 20 more.

But Cohen has been as grabby as any senator in winning defence work for his home state -- especially ships built and repaired at the Bath, Maine, Iron Works and the nearby Portsmouth, New Hampshire, Naval Shipyard.

Military matters brought out Cohen's literary streak at a hearing earlier this year when a U.S. Navy official said defence contractors could not be forced to share trade secrets with each other because that would be like "an open kimono."
The comment seemed to go unnoticed but later in the hearing Cohen came back to it and said he would call his next mystery novel "The Case of the Open Kimono."
Cohen was born on Aug. 28, 1940, in Bangor, Maine, and was educated at the state's elite Bowdoin College.
He has two sons by his first marriage, which ended in divorce. Last Feb. 14 he married Boston television personality Janet Langhart.
